lesson.title: Mapping Every Electron in a Molecule
lesson.summary: A Lewis structure extends the dot symbols of individual atoms into a full diagram of a molecule or polyatomic ion, showing exactly which electrons are shared as bonds and which remain as lone pairs.
lesson.body:
A Lewis dot symbol shows the valence electrons available on one isolated atom. A Lewis structure takes that same bookkeeping and extends it to an entire molecule or polyatomic ion, showing how those valence electrons are actually distributed once atoms bond together, some pairs shared between two atoms as covalent bonds, and some pairs left over as lone pairs belonging to just one atom. Drawing one correctly is a systematic process, not a guessing game, and it follows the same handful of steps every time.

The first step is counting. Add up the valence electrons contributed by every atom in the molecule, using each element's group number the same way used for individual dot symbols. For a polyatomic ion, adjust the total for the overall charge, subtracting one electron for each unit of positive charge, since a cation has fewer electrons than a neutral collection of the same atoms would, or adding one electron for each unit of negative charge, since an anion has extra electrons.

The second step is arranging a skeleton and placing bonds. Typically the least electronegative atom other than hydrogen sits in the center, since it can form the most bonds to surrounding atoms, and hydrogen, which can only ever form one bond, always sits on the outside. Connect each outer atom to the center with a single bonding pair to start, then work outward, giving each terminal atom enough additional lone pairs to complete its own octet, or its duet if that atom is hydrogen. Finally, check whether the center atom also has a complete octet using only the electrons placed so far; if it comes up short, a lone pair on a neighboring atom is converted into an additional bonding pair, upgrading a single bond to a double or triple bond, until every atom's electron count works out.

Water is a compact worked example. Oxygen contributes 6 valence electrons and each hydrogen contributes 1, for a total of 8. Oxygen sits in the center, bonded to the two hydrogen atoms by two single bonds, which uses 4 of the 8 electrons. The remaining 4 electrons become two lone pairs, both placed on oxygen, since hydrogen cannot hold a lone pair. Counting oxygen's total: two bonding pairs, worth 4 electrons, plus two lone pairs, worth 4 more, gives 8, a complete octet. Each hydrogen counts its one bonding pair, 2 electrons, a complete duet. Every one of the 8 counted electrons has been placed, and every atom is satisfied.

This same procedure, count electrons, build a skeleton, distribute bonds and lone pairs, check every atom's octet, works identically for the many other molecules and ions covered from here forward, including how the octet rule sets the target every atom is working toward, and how single and double bonds emerge naturally whenever a single bonding pair alone is not enough to satisfy the central atom.
